content: 1. Studies and predictions regarding the removal of substances from water have been conducted. Health-based values are derived by allocating 20% of the upper bound of the Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI) for a 60 kg adult consuming 2 liters of water per day. For acute health-based values, 100% of the Acute Reference Dose (ARfD) is allocated to water for the same parameters. 2. A default allocation factor of 20% is used to account for the fact that available food exposure data, which suggest low exposure via this route, often exclude information from developing countries where exposure may be higher. Additionally, potential exposure via inhalation from indoor air due to the use of dichlorvos as a domestic insecticide is unknown. 3. As a general principle, pesticide concentrations in water, including dichlorvos, should be kept as low as possible and should not be allowed to increase up to the health-based value. 4. Dicofol, a substance derived from DDT, is being phased out in the USA and is no longer approved for use in the European Union. It is unlikely to reach water unless bound to particulate matter subject to runoff. Dicofol is only slightly soluble in water and binds strongly to soil. Limited data exist on its occurrence in water, and food exposure varies widely depending on local circumstances and usage. 5. Dicofol has been proposed as a persistent organic pollutant under the Stockholm Convention. A health-based value of 2 mg/kg body weight was derived based on a NOAEL of 15 mg/kg body weight for decreased body weight and feed intake in an acute neurotoxicity study in rats, with a safety factor of 100 applied. 6. Dicofol is effectively removed from water by adsorption onto activated carbon, and any dicofol adsorbed onto particulate matter is likely removed during coagulation. 7. Di(2-ethylhexyl) adipate (DEHA) has low short-term toxicity but induces peroxisomal proliferation in the liver of rodents at dietary levels above 6000 mg/kg of feed. This effect is often associated with liver tumor development. DEHA induced liver carcinomas in female mice at very high doses but not in male mice or rats. It is not genotoxic and has been classified by IARC as Group 3 (not classifiable as to its carcinogenicity to humans). 8. A health-based value of 80 µg/L for DEHA can be calculated based on a Tolerable Daily Intake (TDI) of 280 µg/kg body weight, derived from fetotoxicity in rats, with 1% of the TDI allocated to drinking water. 9. DEHA occurs in drinking water at concentrations well below those of health concern, and a formal guideline value has not been established. 10. Di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) is primarily used as a plasticizer. Exposure varies widely due to its incorporation into a broad range of products, with food being the main exposure route. DEHP is readily absorbed in rats but less so in primates, including humans. It is widely distributed in the body, with the highest levels in the liver and adipose tissue, but does not accumulate significantly. 11. DEHP has low acute oral toxicity. In rodents, it causes hepatic peroxisome proliferation, indicated by increased peroxisomal enzyme activity and histopathological changes. Primates, including humans, are less sensitive to this effect. 12. Long-term oral carcinogenicity studies in rodents have shown hepatocellular carcinomas. IARC has classified DEHP as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B). JECFA recommended reducing human exposure to DEHP in food to the lowest attainable level. 13. Dimethoate is an organophosphorus insecticide used in agriculture and for controlling houseflies. It has a half-life of 18 hours to 8 weeks and is relatively stable at pH 2–7. It is not expected to persist in water. 14. Dimethoate inhibits cholinesterase and is a skin irritant in human studies. It is not carcinogenic in rodents. Although in vitro studies suggest mutagenic potential, this is not expressed in vivo. 15. A health-based value for dimethoate was derived based on reproductive toxicity in rats, with a NOAEL of 2 mg/kg body weight per day and an uncertainty factor of 500 applied. 16. 1,4-Dioxane is used as a stabilizer in chlorinated solvents and as a solvent for various industrial and consumer products. It is not removed by conventional water treatment processes but can be effectively removed by biological activated carbon treatment. 17. 1,4-Dioxane has caused hepatic and nasal cavity tumors in rodents in long-term oral studies. Tumors in the peritoneum, skin, and mammary gland were observed in rats at high doses. IARC has classified 1,4-dioxane as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B). 18. Diquat is a non-selective, fast-acting contact herbicide used for weed control in agriculture and residential settings. It is highly soluble in water but strongly adsorbed to soil, making it resistant to degradation in the sorbed state. 19. The primary target organ for diquat toxicity is the eye, with effects also observed on the kidney, liver, and hematological parameters. Diquat is not carcinogenic in rodents and has shown equivocal or positive responses in some genotoxicity tests but was negative in in vivo assays. 20. As a general principle, pesticide concentrations in water, including diquat, should be kept as low as possible and should not be allowed to increase up to the health-based value.
